Design question: Target architecture
Agreed rule / proposed option: Use existing x86 xv6-public tree (PDF 3).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Adapt project mechanisms to real x86 interfaces; do not copy RISC-V prototypes.

Design question: Meaning of speculation ID
Agreed rule / proposed option: One ID identifies one shared attempt, not a process or a type of speculation.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Participants refer to one shared context holding private state. Exact ID allocation/range remains open.

Design question: Whether nested xbegin() is rejected.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Reject nested xbegin with -1.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Check membership before allocation; retain existing ID and changes; child calling xbegin is also nested. A new begin after a completed speculation is allowed.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Owner is the process that successfully calls xbegin.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Record owner identity in shared context; fork does not transfer ownership.

Design question: Fork inheritance
Agreed rule / proposed option: Children inherit the parent speculation ID.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Register child membership safely; descendants share private filesystem changes and held output.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Only owner may call xcommit successfully.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Non-owner: return -1 without changing speculation. Owner also must be sole remaining participant.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Only owner may call xabort successfully in iteration 1.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Non-owner: return -1 unchanged. Any-member abort is a possible future extension, not current policy.

Design question: How commit waits for or stops other participating processes.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Return -1; do not wait, freeze, or terminate peers for an explicit request.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Check all living participants sharing the ID, including descendants, under synchronization; owner retries after they exit.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Release membership after exit cleanup; retain shared speculative changes/output.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Keep association during relevant resource cleanup; detach afterward. Member termination alone does not cancel the group.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: No longer counts as a living participant after exit cleanup/detachment.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Do not require wait/reaping to release speculation membership.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Kernel automatically cancels the speculation; never auto-commit.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Mark ABORTING; reject new work; mark remaining members killed and wake sleeping members; allow safe exit cleanup; reclaim only after all references/in-flight users are gone.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Owner-only syscall permission does not prevent kernel cleanup.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Owner death triggers cancellation independently of xabort permission checks.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Do not free private state while it is in use; do not make surviving workers non-speculative and let them continue.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Coordinate in-flight operations and exit paths; cancellation is not instantaneous; safe cleanup must remain possible in ABORTING.

Design question: Successful explicit completion
Agreed rule / proposed option: After successful commit/abort, owner becomes non-speculative.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Publish or discard shared state, complete safe cleanup, then detach owner. Failure behavior depends on failure category and needs further specification.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: 8 distinct writable shadow blocks per speculation, including metadata (4096 bytes of block data).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Count the complete modified-block footprint, including inode, directory, bitmap and indirect blocks where applicable. Keep limits in named constants; do not hardcode eight in algorithms.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Commit the entire speculation in one durable filesystem-log transaction; maximum footprint is 8 distinct home blocks initially.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Coordinate log reservation/admission and cache resources; ensure actual commit completion before releasing held output. Ordinary end_op returning does not by itself prove durability when operations share a transaction.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Fail with -1 before the next unsupported mutation; never spill changes to real storage.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Define rollback/preflight for a syscall touching several blocks; earlier private work must remain consistent or mark context abort-only. Exact failure semantics require agreement.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Move to a larger shadow cap with a correspondingly larger filesystem log and buffer cache; exact upgraded sizes remain to be selected.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Upgrade shadow capacity, log space/reservation, and cache headroom together; check log-header capacity and rebuild fs.img. Preserve syscall/lifecycle policies. Rerun capacity, crash and concurrency tests. A 64-block shadow cap is a candidate, not an accepted final size.

Design question: Maximum active speculations and ID allocation
Agreed rule / proposed option: No exact count, ID range or reuse policy agreed.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Choose shared-table bound and safe identity reuse; distinct from per-speculation shadow capacity.

Design question: Conflict rule
Agreed rule / proposed option: No final conflict detection/resolution policy selected.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Prior discussion listed options only. Decide before outside writers are supported; block-level metadata conflicts matter too. Interim Step-4 rule agreed as D20 (refuse the outside writer/unlink with -1); the final policy
column6: including two speculations copying the same block at commit

Design question: exec behavior and inherited resources
Agreed rule / proposed option: No final exec / descriptor membership rules selected.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Define exec association and inherited descriptor handling before broader workloads.

Design question: Console and external-pipe capacity
Agreed rule / proposed option: Buffering required; exact sizes/overflow behavior not agreed.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Choose bounds and failure/backpressure rules; preserve same-speculation pipe communication.

Design question: Failure and crash semantics
Agreed rule / proposed option: Atomic file commit required; detailed post-error behavior not fully specified.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Define abort-only cases, cancellation during commit, crash boundary and output delivery limitations.

Design question: Should we reserve shadow-block storage in advance (a fixed pool), or allocate memory only when needed?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Allocate shadow storage dynamically when needed, with a maximum of eight writable shadow blocks per speculation for now.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Keep the limit in a named constant. The context resources pointer refers to the shadow-storage structure; it does not allocate memory itself. Use an extensible layout so a larger cap does not require replacing the storage design. Handle allocation failure and safe cleanup. Raise log/cache limits together before supporting larger commits. Exact page/entry layout will be chosen during implementation.

Design question: How do we stop two members from creating separate private copies of the same block?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Reserve an entry before unlocking. Entries move from FREE (unused) to LOADING (reserved, contents not ready) to READY (safe to access).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Pin the context. Under resource_lock, find an existing entry or reserve one as LOADING; reservations count toward the eight-block cap. Unlock before allocating block storage or reading disk. Relock to finalize READY or release a failed reservation. Coordinate cancellation, wake waiters, and release references safely. Exact page layout and cancellation synchronization remain implementation details.

Design question: Why must we reserve an entry before reading the original block?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Without a reservation, two processes in the same speculation can both think that block 42 has no private copy and create duplicate entries.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Without reservation: A locks, sees no shadow for block 42, unlocks and starts reading disk. B locks, also sees no shadow, unlocks and prepares another copy. With reservation: A marks block 42 LOADING before unlocking. B sees LOADING and waits. A finishes, marks READY and wakes B. B retries and uses the same entry. This prevents duplicate initialization; outside-writer conflicts are a separate later problem.

Design question: Which spinlocks protect the context table and the shadow entries?
Agreed rule / proposed option: ptable.lock protects process membership and context lifecycle metadata. Each context has its own resource_lock to protect private resource bookkeeping, such as shadow-entry lookup, reservation and publication.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Use spec_pin to keep the context alive before using resources, then take resource_lock with ptable.lock released. Release resource_lock before spec_unpin. Do not nest these two spinlocks. Do not hold either across disk I/O or other work that may sleep. A pin protects lifetime; it does not by itself prevent cancellation.

Design question: How should a member wait while another member loads a shadow block?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Wait for a LOADING entry without keeping the resource spinlock held while asleep, then retry the lookup and context checks.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Use the xv6 sleep(channel, lock) handoff or an equivalent synchronized protocol to avoid missed wakeups. sleep releases the supplied lock before sleeping and reacquires it on return. Recheck in a loop after wakeup. Wake waiters on success, allocation failure and cancellation; never expose incomplete data or fall back to a public write. Reading disk does not automatically release an unrelated resource_lock.

Design question: Step 4: What happens when a process outside a speculation writes, truncates or deletes file data that the speculation has privately copied?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Refuse the outside operation with -1 and leave the public file unchanged. The speculation is not affected and continues normally.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Granularity (assistant recommendation adopted with A1): block level for writes - an outside write to a block that any active speculation has a shadow of (READY or LOADING) is refused; writes to other blocks of the same file proceed. File level for freeing - an outside unlink or O_TRUNC of a file of which any active speculation has a shadowed block is refused, so a shadowed block can never be freed and reused by another file. Refusals stop once the speculation commits or aborts. Blocks the speculation only read are not protected (reads are not a snapshot). Two speculations privately writing the same block do not conflict in Step 4; that is a Step 5 commit question. A multi-block outside write refused part-way follows the xv6 short-write convention. Ordinary programs can now get -1 while a speculation runs; this is the accepted cost. Step-4 scoped rule; the final conflict policy O02 remains open. Example: S copies block 42 (Hello -> private World); P's write of Howdy to block 42 returns -1; the public block still says Hello; S continues.

Design question: Step 4: Which open files may a speculating process use for reading and writing regular files?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Only file objects opened by a member of the same speculation, during that speculation. Using a regular-file descriptor opened before xbegin (or by another speculation) returns -1. Console/device descriptors are exempt.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Record the opening speculation ID in struct file at open time; check it in read/write for FD_INODE regular files. Reason: a file object opened before xbegin may be shared with an outside process, and a speculative read/write would move that outsider's offset (a visible effect that survives abort). Children forked after xbegin are members, so they may use the speculation's files. Known cost: files opened before xbegin must be reopened, and shell redirection such as cmd > file gives a pre-opened descriptor that is refused. Per-speculation private offsets are a possible later extension.

Design question: Step 4: What does a speculative write return if it fails part-way (shadow cap reached, out of memory, cancellation)?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Return the number of bytes actually written to the private view; return -1 only if no byte was written. The public file is never changed on any failure path.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Follows the usual xv6/Unix short-write convention. The file offset advances by exactly the bytes written. The speculative path must not hit filewrite's existing short-write panic. The program must check short writes (usually by aborting); a half-updated private view is otherwise possible. No up-front check or rollback is done, because another member can consume free shadow slots concurrently. Step 5 may additionally decide whether a short write makes the speculation abort-only (see R03/O05).

Design question: Step 5: What happens if the owner is killed while xcommit() is running?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Kill wins until publication starts; after that, commit wins. Commit checks for a kill one last time after taking the inode locks and passing validation, just before the first public buffer is changed (the point of no return).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Killed before the point of no return: no public change, the speculation is cancelled (ABORTING) and its private blocks are discarded when the owner exits. Killed after it: commit completes durably and the process then dies on return to user mode; it never sees the 0, but the commit happened and is never described as aborted. Reason: in xv6 a log_write()n buffer joins the shared transaction and cannot be taken back. Cost: a kill during the short publication window cannot stop the commit.

Design question: Step 5: Two speculations privately changed the same block. What happens when they commit?
Agreed rule / proposed option: First committer wins. Each private copy keeps the original bytes it was copied from; at commit, if any public block no longer matches its original, xcommit returns -1 and the speculation becomes abort-only.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Validation and publication run inside one exclusive log transaction with the affected inode locks held; D20 already refuses outside writers, so nothing can change a validated block before it is installed. An abort-only speculation can only xabort (or exit). Step-4 behaviour (two speculations may both privately write a block) is unchanged. Resolves O02 for commit-time conflicts between speculations; broader conflict handling (Step 9) stays open.

Design question: Step 5: Should a partial (short) speculative write make the speculation abort-only? (R03)
Agreed rule / proposed option: No. The program receives the exact byte count (D22) and decides whether to commit what was written.
Action sequence / implementation implica: No abort-only flag is set on short writes. Programs that ignore short write counts may commit a half-updated private view; this is documented. Resolves R03.

Design question: Step 5: What does a crash mean for a speculation that was committing? (part of O05)
Agreed rule / proposed option: Crash before the log header (commit record) reaches disk: recovery yields the complete old file and the speculation is simply gone. Crash after it: recovery yields the complete new file, even if the caller never received xcommit's return value.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Speculation contexts live only in memory and do not survive reboot. The durable point is write_head() of the speculation's own exclusive log transaction. No exactly-once notification to the caller is claimed. Output release (console/pipes, later steps) must wait for this durable point. Other O05 details (output delivery at crash) stay open.

Design question: Step 5: What happens to file offsets of files opened during a speculation after abort?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Leave them as they are. Offsets belong to the members' file objects, not to the public file, and are not rewound on abort.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Documented behaviour, no code. After abort the file contents revert but the offset still reflects the private writes; a program that keeps using such a descriptor must reposition itself (xv6 has no lseek, so reopen).
